segments.arabic:
١٢٠٧٨- أم سليمان بنت أبي حكيم:
يقال: هي والدة سليمان بن أبي حثمة «١» .
وتقدم أن اسمها الشّفاء، وقال: هي غيرها. قال أبو عمر: أم سليمان، وقيل أم سليم العدويّة، وقال بعضهم: أم سلمة. روى عنها عبد اللَّه بن الطّيب أو الطبيب- أنها قالت:
أدركت من النّساء وهن يصلّين مع النّبي ﷺ الفرائض.
قلت: وصله ابن مندة من طريق أحمد بن يونس، عن ابن شهاب، عن ابن أبي ليلى، عن عبد الكريم، عن عبد اللَّه بن فلان، عن أم سليم بنت أبي حكيم- فذكره، ولم يقل في آخره الفرائض. قال: ورواه محمد بن عبد الوهاب، عن ابن شهاب، فقال: عن أم سلمة بنت حكيم.
قلت: رواية بنت عبد الوهاب وصلها الطّبرانيّ في الأوسط، عن موسى بن هارون،
(١) أسد الغابة ت (٧٤٨٠) .
segments.english:
12078 - Umm Sulayman bint Abi Hakim:

She is said to have been the mother of Sulayman ibn Abi Hathma.[1]

It was stated above that her name was al-Shifa; however, it was also said that she was a woman other than al-Shifa. Abu Umar said: “Umm Sulayman”; she was also called Umm Sulaym al-Adawiyya, while some called her Umm Salama. Abd Allah ibn al-Tayyib—or Abd Allah ibn al-Tabib—related from her that she said, “I lived to see [elderly] women performing the obligatory prayers with the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).”

I say: Ibn Mandah connected it by way of Ahmad ibn Yunus, from Ibn Shihab, from Ibn Abi Layla, from Abd al-Karim, from Abd Allah ibn so-and-so, from Umm Sulaym bint Abi Hakim; he then cited the report, but did not include “the obligatory prayers” at its end. He said: “Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab transmitted it from Ibn Shihab, but gave it as: ‘from Umm Salama bint Hakim.’”

I say: al-Tabarani transmitted the narration of the daughter of Abd al-Wahhab with a connected chain in al-Awsat, from Musa ibn Harun,

[1] Usd al-Ghaba, biography no. 7480.

segments.arabic:
عنه. واعتمد الذّهبي على رواية ابن يونس، ففسر القواعد بقواعد إبراهيم، وليس كما ظنّ، بل المراد القواعد من النّساء.
هكذا أخرجه أبو بكر بن أبي شيبة، عن أحمد بن يونس بلفظ: «لا تصلّين الفرائض» .
والسند ضعيف من أجل ابن أبي ليلى، وهو محمد، وشيخه عبد الكريم، وهو ابن أبي المخارق.
وقد أخرجه ابن مندة أيضا في ترجمة أم سليمان بن أبي خثمة، من طريق أبي محصن [ابن حصين] «١» بن نمير، عن ابن أبي ليلى كذلك، فقال: عبد اللَّه بن الطّيب، فذكره.
وأخرجه أبو نعيم من مسند الحسن بن سفيان، عن محمد بن جامع، عن أبي محصن، عن ابن أبي ليلى كذلك.
segments.english:
from him. al-Dhahabi relied on Ahmad ibn Yunus's narration and interpreted qawa'id as the foundations of Ibrahim. That is not as he supposed; rather, what is meant is elderly women.

Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba transmitted it in this form from Ahmad ibn Yunus, with the wording: “You do not perform the obligatory prayers.”

The chain is weak on account of Ibn Abi Layla—namely, Muhammad—and his teacher Abd al-Karim—namely, Ibn Abi al-Mukhariq.

Ibn Manda also transmitted it in the entry for the mother of Sulayman ibn Abi Khathama, through Abu Mihsan [ibn Husayn]¹ ibn Numayr, from Ibn Abi Layla in the same manner. He gave the name as Abdullah ibn al-Tayyib and then related the report.

Abu Nu'aym also transmitted it from Musnad al-Hasan ibn Sufyan, from Muhammad ibn Jami', from Abu Mihsan, from Ibn Abi Layla in the same manner.

names.arabic: عبد الكريم، وهو ابن أبي المخارق

unresolved.explanation: The canonical page reads “the daughter of Abd al-Wahhab,” which the translation retains. The preceding Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the masculine pronoun عنه on the following page make ابن عبد الوهاب plausible, but no supplied al-Isabah witness confirms an emendation.

The statement compares this woman with al-Shifa, but the individual represented by “he said” is not identified by the supplied evidence. The final English therefore uses a neutral passive construction.

The canonical vocalization supports a second-person feminine singular statement, which the final text preserves. The context and Urdu witness favor a third-person description, while collateral Arabic reports have a positive third-person clause; whether the canonical wording is intentional or textually disturbed cannot be determined.
